paragraphs: Preference-based fine-tuning teaches a language model which responses people, or other models acting as judges, prefer. Collecting these comparisons consumes resources, so the choice of examples matters. This paper studies how to choose useful preference examples for Direct Preference Optimization, a method presented as a simpler and more stable alternative to reinforcement learning from preferences.

The authors develop an active learning strategy: rather than treating every available example as equally useful, they score prompt and completion pairs to guide selection. Their acquisition function combines the language model’s predictive entropy with a certainty measure from the implicit preference model that DPO optimizes. These provide different signals about the model’s uncertainty when deciding which examples to learn from.

The reported results show improvements in both learning speed and final fine-tuning performance on pairwise preference data. The contribution therefore concerns how supervision is allocated as well as how it is used: better example selection can make preference labels more valuable within the DPO training process.
icml-2024-active-preference-learning-for.tldr: An active learning strategy selects preference examples for DPO and improves learning speed and final performance.

paragraphs: The Weisfeiler–Leman hierarchy provides a theoretical way to characterize how much graph structure a model can distinguish. Graph architectures designed around its different orders have well-understood expressive power, but that theoretical strength has not consistently translated into leading predictive performance. Applying transformers at higher orders also introduces substantial runtime and memory demands.

This paper strengthens the connection between transformers and the hierarchy, establishing stronger expressivity results for each order while making the constructions more feasible in practice. The motivation includes avoiding impractical architectural requirements in earlier approaches, such as infeasible numbers of attention heads. The authors also develop a framework for analyzing established positional encodings, including Laplacian encodings and SPE.

Experiments on PCQM4Mv2 show predictive performance competitive with the state of the art. Fine-tuning on smaller molecular datasets also produces strong downstream results. Together, the theory and experiments connect formal graph-discrimination capabilities with practical prediction, without claiming that greater expressivity alone guarantees better performance on every graph task.
icml-2024-aligning-transformers-with-wei.tldr: The paper strengthens transformers’ alignment with the Weisfeiler–Leman hierarchy and demonstrates competitive molecular prediction performance.

paragraphs: Autoformalization translates informal mathematical statements and arguments into forms that a computer can verify. Euclidean geometry makes this difficult because a written proof often leaves some information to its diagram. A language model translating only the explicit text must otherwise contend with those unstated geometric relationships.

The paper introduces a framework combining language models, domain knowledge, and SMT solvers. Its central division of work assigns theorem provers the task of filling in diagrammatic information, while the language model formalizes the steps actually expressed in the text. This reduces the amount of implicit reasoning the model must translate. The framework also supports automatic semantic evaluation of formalized theorem statements.

The authors construct LeanEuclid, a benchmark containing problems from Euclid’s Elements and UniGeo formalized in Lean. Experiments with GPT-4 and GPT-4V examine both capabilities and limitations in geometry autoformalization. The contribution is thus a coordinated translation-and-reasoning framework together with a benchmark for assessing how successfully models perform this task.
icml-2024-autoformalizing-euclidean-geom.tldr: A neuro-symbolic framework uses theorem provers to supply diagrammatic information while language models formalize explicit geometry text.

paragraphs: Language model agents must turn instructions into sequences of actions when working with browsers or APIs. Generalizing to a new environment often requires human demonstrations. BAGEL addresses this dependence by constructing synthetic demonstrations from the agent’s own exploration, without human supervision.

The process begins with randomly explored trajectories, meaning sequences of actions in an environment. One language model component labels a trajectory with a synthetic instruction. A second component, a zero-shot agent, attempts that instruction and produces a refined trajectory. Repeating this round trip gradually shifts the initial trajectories toward behavior that natural language can describe well, despite both components being noisy.

At test time, BAGEL retrieves demonstrations relevant to the current instruction and supplies them through in-context learning. The reported experiments on ToolQA and MiniWob++ show absolute improvements described as over 2–13%, alongside reductions in execution failures of up to thirteenfold. These findings support using iterative synthetic demonstration generation to help agents adapt to digital environments.
icml-2024-bagel-bootstrapping-agents-by-.tldr: BAGEL turns random exploration into synthetic demonstrations through repeated language-guided refinement, improving agents without human supervision.

paragraphs: In stochastic rising bandits, selecting an option improves its expected future reward. This represents situations where the options themselves learn, such as choosing among models whose performance improves with use. The paper studies how to spend a fixed number of selections before recommending the best option at the end.

The authors propose two methods. R-UCBE uses an approach related to upper confidence bounds, while R-SR progressively rejects options. Both must address the fact that collecting information also changes the options being evaluated. With a sufficiently large budget, the paper provides guarantees on the probability of identifying the optimal option and on simple regret, the loss associated with the final recommendation.

A lower bound characterizes unavoidable identification error, and R-SR matches it up to constants. The analysis also shows that requiring a sufficiently large budget is intrinsic to this setting. Numerical experiments in synthetic and realistic environments validate the proposed methods, connecting the theoretical guarantees to their observed behavior.
icml-2024-best-arm-identification-for-st.tldr: Two algorithms identify the best improving option under a fixed budget, with guarantees that require sufficiently many selections.

paragraphs: Controlled decoding steers a language model toward rewarded responses using a separate module while keeping the base model frozen. The paper formulates this as a token-level reinforcement learning objective with KL regularization, which balances reward seeking against deviation from the base model’s behavior.

The separate module is a prefix scorer trained to learn a value function for the reward. During generation, it evaluates partial responses and guides subsequent decoding. The paper establishes that controlled decoding samples from a solution to its reinforcement learning objective and reports effective control on benchmarks. This gives the scoring module both an optimization interpretation and an inference-time role.

The authors also demonstrate that scorers for different rewards can be combined without additional training to address multiple objectives. Benefits transfer to an unseen base model without further tuning in their experiments. A blockwise version extends control beyond individual tokens, connecting the approach with best-of-K generation and offering another way to apply the same framework.
icml-2024-controlled-decoding-from-langu.tldr: Controlled decoding uses a learned prefix scorer to steer a frozen language model according to a reinforcement learning objective.

paragraphs: Diffusion Rejection Sampling addresses how to improve generation from an already trained diffusion model. Its focus is the sampling process: the sequence of intermediate transitions through which the model produces a sample. Errors in these transitions motivate a mechanism that checks and refines samples along the way.

The method, called DiffRS, applies rejection sampling to align the model’s transition kernels with the true kernels at each timestep. A transition kernel describes how the sampling process moves from one intermediate state to the next. Viewed operationally, DiffRS evaluates intermediate sample quality and varies the refinement effort according to the sample, rather than assigning identical effort to every generated result.

The theoretical analysis shows that DiffRS can obtain a tighter sampling-error bound than the pretrained models. Experiments report state-of-the-art benchmark performance and demonstrate effectiveness with fast diffusion samplers and large text-to-image models. These results support intermediate rejection and refinement as a way to improve sampling from powerful existing diffusion models.
icml-2024-diffusion-rejection-sampling-6.tldr: DiffRS refines intermediate diffusion samples through rejection sampling, with improved error bounds and strong reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Some sequential decisions require choosing several actions at once, each affecting a different part of a system. The learner can observe each action’s intermediate effect before considering the combined reward. This paper introduces factored-reward bandits for the particular case where the overall reward is the product of those intermediate observations.

The authors derive lower bounds on regret, which measures the cumulative cost of learning instead of making optimal choices. They examine both worst-case difficulty across problems and asymptotic difficulty for a particular problem instance. These perspectives distinguish an algorithm that handles difficult cases well from one that fully exploits the structure of an individual case.

Two algorithms address these objectives. F-UCB is an anytime optimistic method that matches the worst-case lower bound up to logarithmic factors, but is not optimal in the instance-dependent sense. F-Track instead tracks the relevant bound and achieves optimal asymptotic instance-dependent regret. The results clarify what exploiting intermediate observations can achieve under the multiplicative reward structure.
icml-2024-factored-reward-bandits-with-i.tldr: The paper analyzes bandits with multiplicative rewards and intermediate observations, providing algorithms with distinct optimality guarantees.

paragraphs: Graph Attention Networks assign different importance weights to neighboring nodes when combining information. However, choosing which neighbors matter does not necessarily provide enough control over whether neighborhood information should be used at all. The paper shows analytically and experimentally that these networks often struggle to suppress aggregation that is irrelevant to the task.

GATE extends graph attention to address this unnecessary mixing. By reducing contributions from unrelated neighbors, it alleviates over-smoothing, where repeated aggregation makes node representations less distinct. It also allows additional layers to remain useful when aggregation is almost or entirely switched off: those layers can still transform each node’s features through linear or nonlinear operations.

The reported results show that GATE often outperforms GATs on real-world heterophilic datasets, where connected nodes can be dissimilar. The authors also construct a synthetic test bed for studying how well models select the appropriate amount of aggregation. This directly examines the capability at the center of the proposed architectural change.
icml-2024-gate-how-to-keep-out-intrusive.tldr: GATE helps graph attention networks suppress irrelevant neighbor aggregation while retaining useful feature transformations at greater depth.

paragraphs: Randomized graph decomposition divides a graph into clusters while trying to preserve nearby relationships. Classical procedures for planar graphs produce connected clusters of limited diameter and tend to keep close nodes together. This paper asks for an additional fairness property: pairs of nodes separated by comparable distances should face comparable probabilities of being split.

The authors show that classical decomposition procedures do not satisfy this individual fairness requirement. They then introduce algorithms offering different trade-offs between fairness, connected clusters, and an optimal number of clusters. The distinction matters because a general tendency to preserve nearby pairs does not itself ensure consistent treatment of pairs at similar distances.

The theoretical analysis connects improvements to the fairness bounds with resolving a major open problem in metric embeddings. This suggests that strengthening those guarantees may be difficult. Experiments on real planar networks modeling Congressional redistricting demonstrate the algorithms’ efficacy, providing an application where the treatment of relationships across a geographic network is directly relevant.
icml-2024-individual-fairness-in-graph-d.tldr: New planar graph decomposition algorithms trade off individual fairness, cluster connectivity, and cluster-count optimality.

paragraphs: HyperNetworks produce the weights used by another network, and kernel prediction applies this idea to convolutional filters. Earlier theoretical work placed full weight prediction above simpler gating in a hierarchy of multiplicative interactions. This paper reexamines that distinction by asking what gating can express when combined with fixed-weight layers.

The authors give a constructive equivalence between that combination and weight prediction. This qualifies the proposed hierarchy: the surrounding fixed layers matter when comparing the power of gating with generated weights. They also establish an equivalence between a restricted form of HyperNetwork and factorization machines, connecting another pair of model formulations.

The paper complements these constructions with empirical evidence that gating layers can learn to imitate weight prediction layers using a variant of stochastic gradient descent. It also applies the reformulation to image denoising with kernel prediction networks, reducing memory requirements. The contribution therefore links representational equivalence to a practical alternative implementation, while separately testing whether the equivalent behavior can be learned.
icml-2024-is-kernel-prediction-more-powe.tldr: Gating combined with fixed-weight layers can express weight prediction, and the reformulation reduces memory in a denoising application.

paragraphs: Goal-directed planning depends on estimating how long it takes to travel between states. In stochastic environments, earlier definitions of temporal distance can violate the triangle inequality. That property relates a direct distance to the distance of a route through an intermediate state, making its absence relevant to shortest-path reasoning and generalization.

The paper shows that successor features learned through contrastive learning can define a temporal distance satisfying the triangle inequality after a change of variables. The result holds even in stochastic settings. The resulting distance is also computationally efficient to estimate in high-dimensional environments, connecting a useful mathematical property with a learnable representation.

Experiments in controlled settings and benchmark suites evaluate a reinforcement learning algorithm built around these distances. It demonstrates combinatorial generalization, described as stitching together behavior, and sometimes learns faster than earlier methods, including methods based on quasimetrics. The findings support the usefulness of the distance construction without asserting a universal learning-speed advantage.
icml-2024-learning-temporal-distances-co.tldr: Contrastively learned successor features yield an efficient temporal distance satisfying the triangle inequality, supporting demonstrated behavioral stitching.

paragraphs: Collections of specialized language models contain expertise acquired through parameter-efficient fine-tuning. This paper asks how to reuse that expertise on unseen tasks. Its method, PHATGOOSE, learns to route among specialized modules, making adaptive choices for individual tokens at individual model layers.

The routing method is post-hoc: it does not require simultaneous access to the datasets used to train the experts. It requires only a modest amount of extra computation after each expert is trained. This makes the method relevant to combining separately developed specializations, while its fine-grained routing allows the chosen expertise to vary throughout processing.

Across the tested expert collections and zero-shot benchmarks, PHATGOOSE outperforms earlier post-hoc routing methods. In some cases, it also exceeds explicit multitask training, which requires simultaneous data access. Qualitative experiments support the authors’ explanation that adaptive choices across tokens and modules contribute to its performance. The results favor flexible reuse of experts without implying that it always surpasses joint training.
icml-2024-learning-to-route-among-specia.tldr: PHATGOOSE adaptively routes tokens through specialized modules to improve zero-shot generalization without jointly accessing expert training datasets.

paragraphs: Traditional reinforcement learning from human feedback converts pairwise judgments into a reward model that scores individual responses. Nash learning from human feedback instead learns a model that directly compares two responses to the same prompt. It then uses that comparison model to define the objective for language model fine-tuning.

The target is a policy whose responses are preferred against those from competing policies, expressed through a Nash equilibrium of the preference model. For tabular policy representations, the authors introduce Nash-MD, an algorithm based on mirror descent. They prove convergence of its last policy iterate to a regularized Nash equilibrium, rather than stating this guarantee only for an average of earlier policies.

The paper also explores parameterized policies and develops gradient descent algorithms for deep-learning architectures. Experiments on text summarization illustrate the approach’s effectiveness. The tabular convergence result and the summarization experiments provide different forms of support for a pipeline that keeps pairwise preferences central throughout learning.
icml-2024-nash-learning-from-human-feedb.tldr: NLHF fine-tunes language models using a pairwise preference model and a Nash-equilibrium objective, with tabular convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning objectives are typically nonconvex, so a small gradient alone does not establish that learning has avoided a saddle point. Second-order analysis addresses this stronger convergence question. Earlier results considered vanilla policy gradients with unbiased estimates, whereas practical implementations introduce bias in several ways.

This paper analyzes biased policy gradient methods in the infinite-horizon discounted setting. One source of bias is estimating an infinite-horizon objective from finite trajectories. Another is using an approximate value function in actor-critic learning. The analysis covers Monte Carlo trajectory estimates and a double-loop actor-critic algorithm whose inner loop improves the critic through TD(0) learning.

The contribution extends second-order convergence analysis to these practically relevant sources of bias. Separately, the authors establish convergence of TD(0) on Markov chains regardless of the initial state distribution. That result concerns the value-learning component itself, complementing the broader analysis of policy updates that depend on its approximation.
icml-2024-on-the-second-order-convergenc.tldr: The paper develops second-order convergence analysis for biased policy gradients and a double-loop actor-critic method.

paragraphs: Sensitivity sampling compresses a dataset by selecting points according to their individual importance. The goal is a small representative sample that approximately preserves the quantities needed for subsequent computation. This paper studies the sample size required for ℓp subspace embeddings when p lies between one and two.

The authors show that a previous bound is tight when sampling uses plain ℓp sensitivities. They then improve the sampling rule by adding ℓ2 sensitivity information. This augmented rule achieves sample complexity proportional to the dimension divided by the squared approximation tolerance, up to logarithmic factors. The result reaches an optimal linear dependence on dimension in the stated range of p.

This brings sensitivity sampling into a regime previously achieved using Lewis weights and resolves the stated open question for p between one and two. An application to logistic regression also improves the dependence on its complexity parameter μ from quadratic to linear. The gains come from modifying the importance measure used for sampling.
icml-2024-optimal-bounds-for-ell-p-sensi.tldr: Adding ℓ2 sensitivities to ℓp sensitivity sampling achieves optimal dimension-linear sample complexity for p between one and two.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that optimization in scientific machine learning should begin with the geometry of the underlying function space. Its proposed order is to choose an optimization algorithm in an infinite-dimensional setting first, then discretize that algorithm to obtain a computational procedure.

The order matters because it makes the function-level problem the starting point for algorithm design. Discretization becomes a later step that translates the chosen procedure into a finite representation. The authors formalize this viewpoint as a principled framework for designing SciML optimization methods, addressing what they describe as an underdeveloped perspective.

To illustrate the argument, the paper discusses recently proposed state-of-the-art SciML algorithms and shows that they can be derived within this framework. Those examples demonstrate how the viewpoint can explain existing methods as well as guide the search for new ones. The contribution is a design position and its formalization, supported by derivations of established approaches rather than a claim that one optimizer is best for every SciML problem.
icml-2024-position-optimization-in-sciml.tldr: The paper advocates designing SciML optimization in function space before discretization and formalizes that approach as an algorithm-design framework.

paragraphs: Decentralized gradient descent lets users train collaboratively by exchanging and averaging model updates with neighbors in a network. Their raw datasets remain local. This paper examines whether the lack of direct communication between distant users prevents one participant from recovering another participant’s private data.

The authors develop an attack that can reconstruct data belonging to users outside the attackers’ immediate neighborhood. They first attack the gossip averaging protocol underlying the communication process, then extend that reconstruction approach to address the additional challenges of decentralized gradient descent. The result shows that indirect interactions through shared updates can expose information beyond direct communication links.

Experiments on real graphs and datasets demonstrate the attack’s effectiveness. A single attacker or a small group often compromises a surprisingly large number of users in the reported evaluations. The authors also investigate how graph topology, attacker count, and attacker placement affect performance. These findings challenge the assumption that network separation alone provides protection for private training data.
icml-2024-privacy-attacks-in-decentraliz.tldr: A reconstruction attack shows that decentralized learning participants can recover private data from users beyond their immediate neighbors.

paragraphs: Understanding a human instruction and turning it into precise robot actions are different challenges. RoboCodeX addresses the connection between them: it uses multimodal information and generated code to synthesize robotic behavior, aiming to generalize across scenarios and robotic platforms.

The framework organizes code generation as a tree and breaks high-level instructions into object-centered manipulation units. These units incorporate physical considerations, including affordances and safety constraints, so the decomposition includes information about how objects can be manipulated. A specialized multimodal reasoning dataset supports pretraining, while an iterative self-updating method supports supervised fine-tuning. Both are intended to strengthen the mapping from conceptual and perceptual understanding to control commands.

Experiments cover four kinds of manipulation tasks and one embodied navigation task, using simulators and real robots. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across these evaluations. The findings support structured decomposition and code generation as a way to connect multimodal understanding with executable robotic behavior in the tested settings.
icml-2024-robocodex-multimodal-code-gene.tldr: RoboCodeX decomposes multimodal instructions into object-centered units and generates code for robotic manipulation and navigation.

paragraphs: Attribution methods estimate how individual inputs contribute to a model’s decision. White-box methods can do this efficiently by using internal gradient information. This paper identifies a problem with that signal: high-frequency artifacts often contaminate the gradients used to construct the explanations.

The proposed method, FORGrad, filters out these artifacts. It uses cutoff frequencies tailored to the characteristics of each model architecture, making the filtering sensitive to the model being explained. The approach improves the signal supplied to existing white-box attribution methods, allowing those methods to retain their computational advantages while producing better explanations.

The authors report consistent improvements across the existing white-box methods they evaluate. With filtering, these methods compete effectively with more accurate but more computationally demanding black-box approaches. The findings connect explanation quality to the frequency content of the gradient signal and support a better balance between faithfulness and computation. Broader adoption of white-box methods is presented as a hoped-for consequence of that improvement.
icml-2024-saliency-strikes-back-how-filt.tldr: FORGrad filters high-frequency gradient artifacts to improve existing white-box explanations while preserving their computational appeal.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation estimates the cumulative reward a target policy will earn. SaVeR studies which behavior policy should collect the data needed for that estimate in a tabular Markov decision process. The collection process must also satisfy a safety requirement based on a known default policy and its expected cost.

The constraint compares the cumulative cost of the behavior policies used with a constant-factor benchmark based on always running the default policy. The authors first identify problems where even an oracle with knowledge of problem parameters cannot efficiently collect data while meeting this constraint. They then define a tractability condition and establish a lower bound for the setting.

SaVeR approximates the safe oracle strategy. The paper bounds its finite-sample mean squared evaluation error while ensuring satisfaction of the safety constraint. Simulations also show low evaluation error with the constraint maintained. The results connect accurate evaluation with the cost of obtaining information, while explicitly recognizing that efficient safe collection is not possible in every MDP.
icml-2024-saver-optimal-data-collection-.tldr: SaVeR collects data for accurate policy evaluation under a default-policy-based safety constraint, alongside tractability analysis and error guarantees.

paragraphs: Time series collected across different tasks or states can vary for several reasons. Underlying processes may change their activity within a state, while their structure may also differ across states. SiBBlInGS seeks interpretable building blocks that represent these distinctions instead of combining all variability into undifferentiated components.

The method uses graph-based dictionary learning to discover sparse building blocks and their temporal activity traces. It draws on co-activity patterns and relationships both within and between states. The framework allows trial-specific timing changes and controlled structural adaptation across states, helping distinguish components shared across states from those specific to one state.

SiBBlInGS also accommodates states with different numbers of sessions and sessions of unequal duration. Synthetic and real-world examples, including web search and neural data, demonstrate its ability to reveal structure in complex observations and its robustness to noise and missing samples. The contribution combines interpretable decomposition with flexibility for the uneven and variable observations found in multi-state time series.
icml-2024-sibblings-similarity-driven-bu.tldr: SiBBlInGS extracts interpretable time-series building blocks while distinguishing within-state variability from structural changes across states.

paragraphs: This paper studies adaptation to an unknown test task drawn from a finite set of Markov decision processes. It assumes a sufficiently long training phase has already recovered that task set perfectly. The remaining challenge is to minimize regret while learning which task is active and acting effectively within it.

Under a separation condition, each task can be distinguished from another through some state-action pair. The authors derive a lower bound showing that dependence at least linear in the number of tasks is unavoidable under this condition. This identifies a statistical barrier even when the possible tasks themselves are already known.

The paper then introduces stronger assumptions called strong identifiability. These enable algorithms with logarithmic dependence on the number of test episodes and sublinear dependence on the number of tasks simultaneously. The contribution explains how the information available for distinguishing tasks controls adaptation speed: fast test-time learning depends on more than merely having recovered the task collection during training.
icml-2024-test-time-regret-minimization-.tldr: The paper establishes test-time regret barriers under task separation and stronger identifiability conditions that permit faster adaptation.

paragraphs: Constrained Markov decision processes represent reinforcement learning problems with safety requirements. Existing regret analyses for primal-dual algorithms allow constraint violations in one round to be offset by stronger satisfaction in another. Such cancellation can hide unsafe behavior during learning behind a favorable overall accounting.

The paper asks whether primal-dual learning can achieve sublinear regret when violations cannot be canceled this way. The authors first extend a last-iterate convergence result for regularized primal-dual methods to problems with multiple constraints. They then use that result to develop a model-based algorithm for learning in an unknown constrained MDP.

The algorithm provably achieves sublinear regret without error cancellations, providing the stated first affirmative answer to this question. The significance is that the guarantee keeps violations visible rather than erasing them with favorable rounds elsewhere. Sublinear accumulation does not itself mean that every learning round is violation-free; it strengthens the long-run guarantee by changing how errors are counted.
icml-2024-truly-no-regret-learning-in-co.tldr: A model-based primal-dual algorithm achieves sublinear regret in unknown constrained MDPs without canceling violations against safer rounds.

paragraphs: Turnstile streams allow matrix data to change through additions, deletions, and repeated updates to rows, columns, or individual entries. This flexibility makes it useful to construct representative samples while processing updates. The paper develops a method for sampling matrix rows in proportion to their ℓp norms in this setting.

The algorithm returns more than selected row identifiers: it also supplies slightly perturbed versions of the rows and estimates their sampling probabilities with relative error control. Combined with preconditioning, it supports ℓp leverage-score sampling. These properties allow subsampling-based regression coresets to be constructed from turnstile streams with little overhead relative to the corresponding offline methods.

For logistic regression, the framework gives the stated first turnstile algorithm with a one-plus-epsilon approximation using polynomial sketch or subsample size. This improves on earlier constant-factor approximations or sizes exponential in inverse epsilon. The paper also experimentally compares the approach with plain oblivious sketching and leverage-score sampling for ℓp and logistic regression.
icml-2024-turnstile-ell-p-leverage-score.tldr: A turnstile streaming sampler supports regression coresets and a one-plus-epsilon logistic regression approximation with polynomial sketch size.
